title: Elon Musk Acquires Mobile Gas-Power Provider APR Energy
teaser: Musk acquires mobile power firm to solve AI's 'energy crunch,' but the rapid deployment faces massive hurdles from permits and pollution laws.
summary: Elon Musk has acquired New APR Energy LLC, a company specializing in mobile gas and diesel-fired power solutions. This acquisition, estimated to be worth over $1 billion, positions Musk's ventures—like AI data centers—to overcome the long wait times for permanent utility connections. APR provides modular generators (20-500 MW+) that can deliver substantial power in just 15-30 days, allowing data centers to begin operating while grid upgrades are pending. This mobile generation 'bridges' the critical gap between construction and utility completion. However, while fast, the deployment faces major regulatory hurdles, including issues with air pollution, permitting, and compliance with the Clean Air Act, which remains a critical consideration for Musk's future operations.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR APR Acquisition: Elon Musk has acquired New APR Energy LLC, a mobile provider of gas- and diesel-fired power systems. Mobile Generation: APR's modular generators can supply large-scale on-site electricity while permanent grid infrastructure is built. Estimated Value: The purchase price is undisclosed; an estimate above $1 billion comes from a 5% stakeholder's $50.4 million payout. Deployment Risk: No Musk business has been named as user, and comparable turbine operations face permit and pollution disputes. Elon Musk acquired New APR Energy LLC, a provider of mobile gas- and diesel-fired power systems. On May 14, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) ended the transaction's federal competition-review waiting period. An FTC transaction record names Musk as the acquiring person and CF APR Super Holdings LLC as the acquired person. Because permanent grid connections can take years, APR's equipment could supply electricity-hungry AI facilities sooner, although Musk has not identified an intended user. Mobile generation can bridge the period between data-center construction and completed utility infrastructure, but that strategic fit does not establish that any Musk company will deploy APR's fleet. Duos Technologies Group, a former 5% non-voting stakeholder in New APR Energy's parent, received about $50.4 million for that interest. A proportional calculation based on the payout implies a value just above $1 billion , but neither the actual purchase price nor a deployment plan has been disclosed. Even so, no Musk-controlled business has been named as the recipient of APR's assets. xAI, SpaceX, Grok, and the Colossus data-center complex have not been identified as users so far. Why Mobile Power Fits the AI Bottleneck APR Energy markets fast-track power solutions that can deliver reliable energy in 30 to 90 days. Its gas turbines and diesel generators range from 20 megawatts to more than 500 megawatts. Operators can add generating blocks as electricity demand rises instead of waiting for one permanent plant to reach full capacity. APR's modular design lets a project start with the capacity its first computing phase needs and expand alongside additional servers. For comparison, xAI's 19-turbine Colossus 2 expansion added mobile generation at another Musk-linked site, although no evidence connects those units to APR. Temporary generators can keep a data center supplied while permanent grid infrastructure is built. Electricity produced on the customer's side of the utility meter reduces immediate reliance on public-grid capacity. APR describes this bridging power as delivering large-scale electricity within weeks. In practice, APR Energy's modular systems have a claimed 15-to-30-day installation window, far less than the years a new utility connection can require. Computing equipment can begin operating before every permanent utility upgrade is finished. Mobile generation changes the construction sequence rather than removing the long-term grid requirement. One company-supplied example shared by APR delivered 250 megawatts in under 30 days for an AI training system. APR's example is not an independent benchmark, but it illustrates the appeal of buying an operator instead of individual machines. APR owns and maintains turbines, transformers, fuel systems, controls, and related equipment, providing one managed package instead of separate hardware purchases and service contracts. Despite that deploymend speed, a prepared site, fuel supply, and electrical connection are still required before the turbines can serve a data center. APR's fast-track solutions are scalable from 20-500 MW+, so owning the operator could remove a procurement step without eliminating those physical requirements. Although SpaceX has separately stated that its data-center operations depend on natural gas and turbine technology, nothing identifies so far SpaceX or its AI division SpaceXAI as APR's customer or establishes a site, schedule, or permanent role. Fast Power Meets Permit and Pollution Risk Because turbines can remain in one place, rapid installation shifts part of the infrastructure challenge from grid access to siting, fuel, air rules, and permits. Musk-linked Colossus 1 and 2 data centers have used natural-gas turbines without permits. No evidence places APR's fleet at those facilities, so the dispute illustrates an equipment-category risk rather than an APR deployment. An EPA ruling on xAI's Memphis turbines addressed earlier operations but does not establish an APR deployment. Nearby residents filed a lawsuit over air pollution caused by turbine operations. Federal intervention in the related Clean Air Act lawsuit adds an unresolved legal constraint to existing Musk-linked operations, although APR Energy's future deployments are not part of those proceedings. Mobile equipment can move between sites, but prolonged operation at one location can still trigger disputes over applicable air rules and permits. Beyond permitting, environmental groups estimate that xAI's turbines could emit more than 2,000 tons of nitrogen oxides. The estimate explains why communities may treat fast gas generation as an air-quality issue rather than only an infrastructure shortcut.

title: Mozilla speeds Firefox release schedule to biweekly
teaser: Mozilla is cutting Firefox's release schedule in half starting in 2026, while the 153 update brings major PDF improvements and crucial EU-level security features.
summary: Mozilla is significantly accelerating its development cycle, planning to move Firefox desktop and Android releases from a 4-week to a 2-week cadence starting in September 2026. Meanwhile, the upcoming Firefox 153 (scheduled for July 21) brings major functional and security updates. Key features include enhanced PDF editing, allowing users to merge multiple documents and insert images. In terms of compliance, 153 supports the EU's Qualified Website Authentication Certificates (QWACs) for eIDAS legislation. The release is also critical as the next ESR version, guaranteeing security updates for at least 15 months (until late 2027). However, users should note that extensions will lose local-file access by default, though the browser introduces other improvements like experimental JPEG XL support and better HDR video playback.
content: SOFTWARE Mozilla speeds Firefox release schedule to biweekly And what to expect in Firefox 153 as the next ESR release gets close Firefox releases will soon get even closer together - but not ESR ones, which remain annual, with the next one due out soon. The change was announced last week on the dev-platform@mozilla.org mailing list by Mozilla's director of engineering Sylvestre Ledru : "We are planning to move Firefox Desktop and Android from a 4-week release cadence to a 2-week release cadence starting in September 2026. "This will be an experiment... This does not mean that all work needs to ship twice as fast. Work that is not ready should not be rushed, and features can still take the time they need to bake. "The current target is to release Firefox 155 on September 1, 2026, instead of September 15 ... "We will closely monitor how this change works in practice and adjust if needed." The change is already visible in the upcoming Firefox Release Calendar . At the time of writing, it shows the current four-week cadence for Firefox 153 and 154, with Firefox 155 brought forward to September 1. From then on, it lists releases at roughly two-week intervals. This isn't unprecedented. The last time Mozilla did it was over a decade ago . Google announced a very similar change for Chrome back in March, and The Register reported on it going to six-weekly releases in 2010 and then four-weekly ones in 2021 . Brace for the impact of the next ESR In the meantime, Firefox 153 is nearly here: at the time of writing, it's scheduled for Tuesday, July 21. Right now, the release notes are blank, but the beta release notes are more forthcoming. You can look forward to further improvements to PDF editing. Version 153 will be able to merge multiple PDF documents into one by a simple drag-and-drop in the PDF sidebar, and insert images into PDFs as new pages. It will also improve highlighting text in PDFs. The new version can generate QR codes for sharing web pages offline, such as in printed documents. It can verify and display the EU's new Qualified Website Authentication Certificate s, or QWACs for short. These are part of the new eIDAS legislation , which is a slightly convoluted acronym for "electronic IDentification, Authentication and trust Services". Sounds cumbersome, but if it helps make the Wild West of the Web a bit safer, we're all for it. Another security tweak is that extensions will lose local-file access by default. As we use one that relies on it - the excellent Multithreaded Download Manager - that's slightly concerning, although users will be able to grant the permission separately, so we'll see. If a tab is using your location, Firefox 153 will highlight this with a map-pin icon in the address bar. The last release could recognize a few keywords in the address bar to mute all sound: this function will get extended, with typed commands for picking colors from pages, and accessing experimental "Labs" features. Come back, Ubuntu Unity and your HUD , all is forgiven. There's also experimental JPEG XL support. Pop-up video player controls will work better, and if you use Windows and have a compatible GPU and drivers, 153 will play HDR video. On macOS, Firefox supports the Fn+F keystroke for switching to full-screen mode - which means KeyboardControls.com has to update its description of the function. Firefox 153 will also be a significant release, because it will be the next ESR version: it will get security updates for at least 15 months , meaning until late 2027. (And maybe longer: Firefox 115 is still getting updates, and now will until March 2027 .) In turn, that means that Firefox 153 is also the basis of the latest beta of the AI-free Waterfox fork , which recently integrated built-in ad blocking . ®

title: EY re-envisions RAG around multimodal knowledge graphs to improve accuracy
teaser: EY unveils a multimodal RAG framework that links text, charts, and diagrams into a knowledge graph, dramatically boosting LLM accuracy.
summary: EY introduced a multimodal RAG framework to overcome the limitations of traditional, text-only Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Because critical facts are often embedded in diagrams, charts, and tables, EY’s system ingests these 'illustrations' and links them to relevant text via a sophisticated knowledge graph. This architecture performs a multi-stage retrieval, storing content in separate indexes before establishing weighted relationships between text and visuals. Dipanjan Sengupta, an AI engineering leader at EY, notes that this enables multi-hop reasoning, providing a more complete and verifiable context for LLMs, especially when guiding AI agents to make better decisions.
author: Paul Gillin
content: Retrieval-augmented generation is a standard way to ground large language models in enterprise information, but new research from EY , the business name of Ernst & Young LLP, says most implementations overlook a lot of useful data. Conventional RAG systems are built mainly to retrieve text. Enterprise documents, however, often place critical facts in charts, tables, engineering diagrams, equations and images. EY has developed a multimodal RAG framework that retrieves those materials alongside text and connects them through a knowledge graph, producing answers that are more complete, contextualized and easier to verify. The approach doesn't affect the underlying LLM, but rather changes how enterprise content is prepared, indexed, related and supplied to the model at inference time. The work grew out of limitations EY encountered in client projects, said Dipanjan Sengupta (pictured), EY Global Delivery Services Consulting distinguished technologist and AI engineering leader. "RAG works well for textual content," he said, "but in many industries, a lot of information is in illustrative content as well." For example, an industrial company may keep essential specifications in engineering drawings, while a life sciences company may rely heavily on graphs. EY's methodology links illustrations back to relevant text, resulting in a "manyfold" increase in accuracy with improved response narratives, Sengupta said. Multiple pipelines The framework begins by separating textual and illustrative content into different ingestion pipelines. Text is segmented and enriched through keyword extraction and named-entity resolution, a process that links records or name variations that represent the same real-world entity. Illustrations are assigned descriptive metadata using existing captions, nearby text, bounding-box analysis, optical character recognition and descriptions generated by a language model. The system stores text and illustrations in separate vector indexes, narrowing the search space and allowing a query to target text, images or both. At the same time, each content element becomes a node in a knowledge graph with weighted relationships connecting relevant passages and illustrations. "We establish relationships between the various illustrations and the text segments," Sengupta said. "We stored the information in a graph database where we had individual nodes for illustrations and for text and rules for establishing the relationships between the two." The white paper describes three methods for building those relationships: deterministic keyword matching, semantic similarity based on embeddings, and machine learning-based inference for implicit associations. A "gleaning" process looks for missing links, resolves ambiguous entities and identifies related information across documents. The result is a heterogeneous graph that can support multi-hop reasoning without requiring the LLM to infer every connection. Retrieval also occurs in stages. The system performs a similarity search against the appropriate modality-specific index. It then uses the resulting identifiers to traverse neighboring nodes in the knowledge graph. The search can remain local, broaden into graph communities or combine both approaches. A multimodal re-ranker orders the retrieved passages and illustrations before inserting them into the LLM prompt. "We are not just relying on vector search but also enhancing the content space to other modes of information," Sengupta said. "That gives us a larger narrative." 'Far better decisions' The configuration process differs from that of many RAG deployments. A compliance application may favor narrow, deterministic retrieval, while a research application may benefit from broader semantic exploration. EY argues that chunking methods, embedding models, relationship-building techniques, reranking strategies and retrieval scope should be configurable rather than hard-coded. Flexibility is one reason Sengupta favors an enterprise platform rather than isolated RAG projects. Common services for ingestion, security, governance and retrieval can be reused while individual business units tune the system for their requirements. The framework could become more important as enterprises deploy artificial intelligence agents. Those need current, domain-specific information to make decisions and select actions, and weak retrieval can propagate errors throughout an automated workflow. "When RAG is enriched with multimodal capability, we find that the agents are far better equipped to make decisions," Sengupta said. RAG can also improve the path an agentic workflow takes. EY's paper presents the method as a foundation for more transparent and domain-aware enterprise RAG, but it does not publish comparative benchmarks or quantify the accuracy gains. The evidence so far is client experience and the presumption that an architecture that retrieves connected visual and textual evidence should produce richer answers than text-only search. Sengupta rejected the idea that expanding model context windows will make RAG unnecessary. Larger windows may reduce the need to split documents into small chunks, he said, but they do not solve the problem of finding the most relevant evidence. Without focused retrieval, an LLM is still searching for "that proverbial needle in the haystack." title: Protecting Public Officials From Doxxing and Online Threats
teaser: Doxxing and online threats pose severe risks to public officials, requiring proactive strategies to safeguard their digital footprint and personal lives.
summary:
Public officials face escalating digital risks, including doxxing (publishing private information without consent), harassment, and identity theft, which can undermine both their personal lives and public confidence. Due to their visible positions, they are attractive targets for opponents, cybercriminals, and activists.

Protecting them requires a proactive digital strategy. Key measures include regularly reviewing online profiles and public records to identify vulnerabilities. Specialized privacy services and robust cybersecurity practices (like multi-factor authentication) are essential. Organizations must also play a key role by providing mandatory training and establishing clear incident response plans for harassment or doxxing. The goal is to balance essential governmental transparency with the right to personal safety, recognizing that sensitive personal data is rarely needed for public accountability.
author: Contributor
content: Public service has always required resilience, but today's officials face challenges that extend far beyond public meetings, policy decisions, and media scrutiny. As government operations become increasingly digital, public officials are finding themselves exposed to new forms of risk that can affect both their professional responsibilities and personal lives. Online harassment, identity theft, impersonation, and doxxing have emerged as serious threats that can undermine safety, privacy, and public confidence. The internet has created valuable opportunities for transparency and citizen engagement, but it has also made personal information easier to access and exploit. Public officials often maintain visible online profiles and interact with constituents through digital platforms, creating a larger digital footprint than many private citizens. As a result, protecting personal information has become a critical component of modern public-sector security. Understanding the Growing Risk of Doxxing Doxxing occurs when an individual's private information is collected and shared publicly without consent. This information may include home addresses, phone numbers, family details, workplace information, or other identifying records. While some of this information may already exist in public databases, gathering and publishing it in one place can create significant security concerns. For public officials, the consequences of doxxing can be particularly severe. Individuals serving in government positions often make decisions that affect communities, businesses, and organizations. Those who disagree with these decisions may attempt to intimidate or pressure officials by exposing personal information online. The danger extends beyond simple privacy violations. Doxxing can lead to harassment, threats, stalking, and attempts to disrupt both professional and personal lives. In some cases, family members may also become targets, making digital privacy a concern that affects entire households rather than just the official involved. Why Public Officials Are Attractive Targets Public officials occupy highly visible positions that naturally attract attention. Whether they work in local government, law enforcement, public administration, education, or the judicial system, their decisions can impact large groups of people. This visibility often makes them attractive targets for individuals seeking attention, influence, or retaliation. The growing availability of online information has made it easier for bad actors to gather personal details. Government websites, social media accounts, public records, and news articles can all contribute to a digital profile that reveals more information than intended. When combined, these sources can provide a detailed picture of an individual's personal and professional life. Today's threats come from a variety of sources. Political opponents, cybercriminals, fraudsters, activists, and organized harassment groups may all use online information to pursue their goals. Advances in technology have also introduced new concerns, including fake profiles, impersonation attempts, and AI-generated content designed to mislead or damage reputations. Building a Comprehensive Digital Protection Strategy Protecting public officials requires a proactive approach rather than reacting after an incident occurs. The first step is understanding what information is already available online. Conducting regular reviews of search results, social media profiles, public records, and data broker listings can help identify potential vulnerabilities before they are exploited. Privacy management should be treated as an ongoing process. Information constantly appears across websites, databases, and online directories. Without continuous monitoring and maintenance, personal information can quickly become widely accessible. Maintaining awareness of an individual's digital footprint is essential for reducing long-term risk. Many organizations are turning to specialized privacy protection services to strengthen security efforts. Solutions such as VanishID Public Sector Protection help public officials identify exposed information, remove sensitive data where possible, and monitor emerging threats. Combined with strong cybersecurity practices such as multi-factor authentication and secure password management, these measures create a stronger defense against online attacks. The Role of Organizational Support While individual officials can take important steps to protect themselves, organizations also play a vital role in reducing risk. Government agencies and public institutions must recognize that digital threats are now a workplace security issue that deserves dedicated resources and attention. Training is one of the most effective forms of protection. Officials and employees should understand how attackers gather information, conduct phishing campaigns, and exploit publicly available data. Increased awareness allows individuals to recognize risks earlier and make better decisions regarding online activity. Organizations should also establish clear response plans for incidents involving doxxing, harassment, or cyber threats. Access to legal support, cybersecurity expertise, communications guidance, and security resources can help officials respond quickly and effectively when problems arise. A coordinated response often reduces the impact of an incident and helps prevent further escalation. Balancing Transparency and Personal Privacy Transparency remains a fundamental principle of public service. Citizens expect accountability and access to information about the individuals who represent them. However, transparency should not require public officials to sacrifice their personal safety or expose their families to unnecessary risk. A distinction must be made between information that serves a legitimate public purpose and information that simply increases vulnerability. Personal contact details, residential addresses, family information, and other sensitive records rarely contribute to public accountability, yet they can create significant security concerns when widely accessible. Finding the right balance requires thoughtful policies and modern privacy practices. Governments and institutions must continually evaluate how information is collected, stored, and shared while ensuring that public access requirements remain intact. Effective privacy protections can coexist with transparency when they are implemented carefully and consistently. Creating a Safer Digital Environment for Public Service The digital landscape continues to evolve, creating new opportunities for public engagement alongside new security challenges. Public officials must navigate an environment where personal information can spread rapidly and where online threats can have real-world consequences. Addressing these risks requires a commitment to both personal vigilance and organizational preparedness. Strong cybersecurity measures, privacy management strategies, employee education, and institutional support all contribute to a safer environment for those serving the public. By taking proactive steps to reduce exposure and respond effectively to threats, government organizations can better protect the individuals who dedicate their careers to public service. Conclusion Protecting public officials from doxxing and online threats is no longer an optional consideration. As digital platforms continue to shape how governments operate and communicate, safeguarding personal information has become an essential part of maintaining security, effectiveness, and public trust. Officials who understand their digital exposure and actively manage their online presence are better positioned to focus on their responsibilities without unnecessary risk. Creating meaningful protection requires collaboration between individuals, organizations, and policymakers. When strong privacy practices, cybersecurity measures, and support systems work together, public officials can engage with their communities confidently while minimizing vulnerabilities. A safer digital environment benefits not only public servants but also the institutions and communities they serve. title: Pebble founder Eric Migicovsky says his 30-day warranty is all about trust
teaser: Despite a short 30-day warranty, Pebble founder Eric Migicovsky cites 'trust' as the key selling point for the relaunched smartwatch line.
summary: Pebble founder Eric Migicovsky defended the brand's relaunched e-paper smartwatches, emphasizing that 'trust' is their most critical asset despite a relatively short 30-day warranty. While the new watches offer updated tech and larger displays, Migicovsky addressed customer concerns over hardware issues, such as glass cracking. To address this, Pebble has replaced 330 Time 2 watches for free out of over 19,000 in the field and committed to continuing free replacements for reasonable reports of glass cracking. The company is also looking into offering replacement parts for DIY repairs. Migicovsky cautioned that the product is a 'grassroots, bottoms-up relaunch' and cannot be guaranteed the same longevity or support infrastructure as polished major competitors. Consumers should expect a product that works great but is not meant to be compared to industry giants.
author: Stevie Bonifield
content: Pebble founder Eric Migicovsky says buyers of its new e-paper smartwatches should know what they're signing up for and trust Pebble to make things right if they run into issues, despite the short warranty. "I think the most important thing is trust," Migicovsky told me in an interview this week. "Do people trust the product that we're making and do they trust the company and the people behind it?" Migicovsky revived Pebble early last year, after the original company shut down in 2016. The new generation of Pebbles has the same aesthetic, but with updated tech, including larger e-paper displays. I was excited about Pebble's return after missing out on the originals, but hesitated after noticing their 30-day warranty. That's about as long as the Pebble Time 2's battery life, so you might not even need to charge it before it's no longer covered. While I ended up ordering a Pebble Round 2 that I'm still waiting for, others have also raised concerns about the watches' warranty. People have also reported running into hardware issues early on, like the front glass cracking on the Pebble Time 2. Earlier this week, Migicovsky addressed the issues in a blog post , saying Pebble has replaced 330 Time 2 watches for free so far, out of over 19,000 watches "in the field." Pebble's blog says it will "continue replacing reasonable reports of glass cracking for free as long as we can. At some point, we will shift to offering a replacement at a highly discounted amount." Additionally, Pebble is "looking into" offering replacement parts so people can do DIY repairs on their watches. While Migicovsky hasn't offered a timeline for when a shift might happen, he emphasized to The Verge that "an immensely small percentage" of watches have had this issue, adding, "It's, for all intents and purposes, no skin off our back whatsoever to just offer straight up free replacements for anyone who has a problem." There's just certain things that we could sign up to do, and there's certain things that we couldn't. "At every step of the way we've communicated, over-communicated about what to expect [and] what the product's going to be like." Pebble warned customers in its announcement for the Pebble 2 Duo and Pebble Time 2 that they shouldn't buy one if they need a "perfectly polished smartwatch," noting that "Things could not last as long as you'd like." "This is effectively a grassroots, bottoms-up relaunch of something that we love, and really wanted to see exist in the world," Migicovsky told me. "In terms of how we support the product, there's just certain things that we could sign up to do, and there's certain things that we couldn't." "You can expect a product that's going to work great, and something that will make you smile, but we can't guarantee it for maybe the length that other companies or other consumer product companies could with their supply chains and networks of stores all around the world to help with replacements. We just don't have that." "It's a Pebble, through and through," Migicovsky says. "If you enjoyed the first go around, you're going to love the second go around. But that having been said, it's not exactly the same as the first era." title: Nuclear startup Valar Atomics in talks to raise new funding at $6B valuation
teaser: Nuclear energy is rebooted for the AI boom: Valar Atomics is set to raise $1B at a $6B valuation, partnering with Nvidia to power data centers.
summary: Nuclear startup Valar Atomics, specializing in Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), is reportedly raising a $1 billion equity round at a $6 billion valuation. The company's pivot toward the AI boom has revitalized nuclear energy, driven by intense data center electricity demands. Valar has partnered with Nvidia to develop nuclear power solutions for future AI data centers. Valar's technology utilizes a helium-cooled, high-temperature gas reactor. Previously, the company raised $450 million at a $2 billion valuation. Furthermore, Valar has challenged the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) in a legal battle over overly long licensing processes. The founder, Isaiah Taylor, has successfully launched multiple startups, positioning Valar as a key player in providing scalable power infrastructure.
author: Marina Temkin
content: Valar Atomics, a startup building small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs) - essentially miniaturized, factory-built power plants designed to be cheaper and faster to deploy than traditional reactors - is in talks to raise a new round of capital, according to three sources familiar with the company. The three-year-old company is seeking a valuation of about $6 billion, and Sequoia is expected to lead the deal, the people said. The Information was the first to report the funding discussions, including that the El Segundo, California, startup is raising a $1 billion equity round. Part of that capital has been raised previously at a lower valuation, the people told TechCrunch. Specifically, Valar has raised $450 million - including $340 million in equity and $110 million in debt - at a $2 billion valuation, per a Bloomberg report in March. Deals structured in multiple installments at varying valuations, occasionally executed at different times, are becoming increasingly common in today's AI-fueled fundraising environment. These deals can create the perception that capital was invested at a single, uniform valuation. In reality, investors in the same round can end up paying different prices for the same company - a distinction that matters more than ever as outsiders try to benchmark red-hot startups against one another. Sequoia and Valar Atomics declined to comment. Earlier this month, the company showed that its nuclear reactor provided a small amount of power to an Nvidia AI chip. Concurrently with that proof-of-concept demonstration, Valar and Nvidia announced a partnership to explore the development of nuclear energy to power future AI data centers. Valar's rise is playing out against a broader demand crunch. Data center electricity needs are projected to grow sharply over the next several years, and utilities in many regions are years away from adding enough new capacity. That vacuum has turned nuclear power - long plagued by cost overruns and regulatory bottlenecks - into one of the more closely watched corners of the AI infrastructure boom. Valar counts Palmer Luckey, the Anduril founder, and Shyam Sankar, Palantir's chief technology officer, among its backers. Others chasing the opportunity include Kairos Power and TerraPower (backed by Bill Gates), which are building next-generation reactors aimed at tech and industrial customers, and NuScale Power, the only SMR developer with U.S. regulatory design approval. (Last year, it won approval for an upgraded, higher-output reactor design.) Valar's technology is based on a helium-cooled, high-temperature gas reactor. The company says it eventually plans to build hundreds of SMRs to power data centers. But while SMRs are theoretically cheaper to manufacture than traditional reactors, the technology is still nascent and it's not at all clear how long it will take to be deployed at industrial scale. In the background, Valar has taken an aggressive legal stance toward its regulator. Last year, it joined several states and rival startups in suing the Nuclear Regulatory Commission , arguing the agency wrongly applies the same lengthy licensing process to small test reactors that it uses for full-size commercial plants. (The case hasn't been unresolved, with both sides repeatedly pausing litigation, which suggests some kind of settlement is in the works.) The company was founded by Isaiah Taylor, who dropped out of high school when he was 16. The now-27-year-old has said he launched two startups before Valar and proudly shared that his great-grandfather worked as a nuclear physicist on the Manhattan Project.

title: TikTok is testing an AI likeness detection tool
teaser: TikTok is testing a new AI tool allowing creators to detect and report content that falsely uses their likeness.
summary: TikTok is rolling out an opt-in detection tool allowing creators to report AI-generated content that mimics their likeness. Initially tested with select US creators, the system requires users to verify their identity through Jumio using a real-time selfie and ID check. After verification, TikTok's system scans for unauthorized AI usage of the creator's likeness. According to TikTok, the facial information is strictly used for likeness matching and identifying misuse, and ID documents are not retained. This tool follows a similar AI detection system recently released by YouTube.
author: Jay Peters
content: TikTok is starting to test an opt-in tool that scans for AI likenesses and lets creators report them to the company, as spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra . The tool is initially being tested with "some" US creators, TikTok US spokesperson Zachary Kizer tells The Verge . YouTube has been working on a similar tool and recently made it available to all adult users . Creators who are part of TikTok's test and want to use the tool will first have to verify their identity with a company called Jumio . You'll have to do a real-time selfie scan and an ID check, but Kizer says that "TikTok does not retain ID documents, and facial information is used only for likeness matching and to help identify potential unauthorized uses of a creator's likeness." After verification, TikTok's system scans for AI-generated content potentially using a creator's likeness. From there, a creator can review what TikTok found and potentially report unauthorized posts and accounts.

title: Inference cloud operator General Compute raises $400M in debt financing
teaser: AI infrastructure sees major capital influx ($400M funding), while industry experts warn that insufficient capital, not compute, is throttling data center growth.
summary: The AI infrastructure market is undergoing significant capital expenditure, highlighted by General Compute Inc. securing $400 million in debt financing to expand its cloud capacity. General Compute distinguishes itself by basing its inference platform on chips from AMD and SambaNova Inc., optimizing for both the prefill phase (AMD MI300X) and decoding (SambaNova). Separately, industry analysis points to a fundamental systemic constraint: a lack of capital, rather than power or compute, is slowing data center deployment. Andrew Sobko of Argentum AI details this 'capital stack' bottleneck, explaining that Argentum's 'demand-first' model accelerates projects by securing contracts and capital upfront, allowing developers to rapidly deploy infrastructure and capitalizing on the surging demand for AI compute.
author: Maria Deutscher
content: Artificial intelligence infrastructure startup General Compute Inc. today announced that it has secured $400 million in debt financing. Upper90, the investment firm that is underwriting the round, will initially provide the company with $100 million. General Compute plans to draw down additional funds as customer demand increases. Unlike most AI infrastructure providers, General Compute is not using Nvidia Corp. graphics cards. The company has based its cloud platform on chips from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and SambaNova Inc., a fellow startup that recently raised $1 billion in funding. AI models answer user prompts through a two-step workflow. They start by extracting the meaning of a prompt, a step known as the prefill phase. They then generate a response one token at a time in a process known as decoding. The decoding phase requires AI models to move a significant amount of data between the host chip's memory and processing circuits. SambaNova's accelerators are specifically optimized to speed up that workflow. As a result, they can perform decoding faster than some Nvidia graphics cards. The speed at which data moves between a chip's memory and processing modules depends on the physical distance between the circuits. The closer they are to each other, the less time it takes data to complete the trip. The memory and processing circuits in SambaNova's chips are placed immediately next to one another, which minimizes data travel times. General Compute uses SambaNova silicon to run decoding calculations. It performs the other step involved in inference workflows, the prefill phase, using AMD's MI300X graphics card. The chip contains 12 dies and eight memory stacks that together contain 153 billion transistors. The MI300X and SambaNova's chips are designed to run in standard air-cooled server racks. As a result, General Compute can add capacity to its cloud without investing in the pricey liquid cooling equipment that most graphics cards require. That translates into faster infrastructure upgrades. General Compute enables customers to access its inference hardware through two services. The first offers managed versions of open-source language models. Developers can access the models through an application programming interface modeled after the one used by OpenAI Group PBC, which eases the learning curve. General Compute's second service provides dedicated infrastructure environments with more computing capacity. The company will use its debt financing to expand its cloud. According to a document on its website, General Compute has inked agreements that give it the option to purchase 15 megawatts' worth of air-cooled rack capacity in co-location facilities. The company expects that infrastructure to be sufficient for its fourth-quarter growth plans.
